You pick a topic and the tutor plays the person in it — the interviewer, the waiter, the doctor — holds the whole conversation in English , and asks you questions on that topic. The moment you make a grammar or word-choice mistake it corrects you in Hinglish , so you always understand why: "'He go' ki jagah 'He goes' bolna chahiye, kyunki he ke saath 's' lagta hai." Built for the ZenBricks take-home assignment, for Priyanka. Only Sarvam AI models are used: Saaras v3 (speech-to-text), sarvam-105b-conversations (LLM), Bulbul v3 (text-to-speech). No other model provider is involved. What it does # Requirement Where 1 Voice in, voice out (STT → LLM → TTS) tutor.Tutor.turn() 2 Understands Hindi and Hinglish; helps when the learner is stuck stuck-learner rule in SYSTEM_PROMPT , answered in Hinglish 3 Role-played conversation on a learner-picked topic persona per topic (interviewer, waiter, doctor…) + session loop 4 Corrects grammar/word-choice, explanation in Hinglish English reply on EN: , Hinglish explanation on HI: 5 Adapts difficulty to the learner's level confidence question in the first message sets LEVEL , re-judged every turn 6 Ends with a written summary: mistakes, corrections, 3 practice items End session button 7 Simple UI vanilla JS ( static/ ) on a stdlib server ( server.py ) + A live voice agent, not a chat box ears and mouth always on: static/app.js + static/vad.js + Five voices to choose from, with a preview Voice select + POST /api/preview + Turn ends after 0.25 s of silence; one icon mutes the mic TurnWatcher in static/vad.js , tested in tests/ Run it git clone https://github.com/astromanish/spoken-english-tutor.git cd spoken-english-tutor python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt export SARVAM_API_KEY=... # https://dashboard.sarvam.ai → API keys .venv/bin/python server.py # → http://127.0.0.1:7860 Press Start and her ear opens while her first line plays out loud: she introduces her character and asks how confident you are speaking English, on a scale of 1 to 5 — that answer sets how much she corrects you. Then just talk. She answers out loud, asks the next thing, and keeps going; End writes the summary. The Voice picker offers five of bulbul:v3's 37 speakers, described by character rather than by name — Warm female · Calm female · Young female · Professional male · Mature male — because the tutor is Priyanka either way; the choice is how she sounds, not who she is. Preview speaks a two-line sample in that voice (one English line, one Hinglish line, so you hear both before committing) — and the sample introduces itself as Priyanka for the female voices and Priyank for the male ones. The pick is remembered in localStorage and travels with the session as a speaker field; an unknown or retired one falls back to the default rather than failing the start. There is no text box and no transcript log. The ear stays open the whole session, including while she is speaking — if you talk over her she stops mid-sentence and takes what you said instead. The round mic button closes the microphone for real — the track is stopped, so the OS indicator goes out — and shows a crossed mic while it is closed. ffmpeg on your PATH converts the fallback recording (a browser upload posted to /api/turn ) into the 16 kHz WAV that Saaras expects; without it, WAV uploads still work and the streaming path is unaffected. The live loop Everything the browser does each ~256 ms block of microphone audio: Level → an RMS, which drives the orb and the turn-taking. Speech → the PCM goes to POST /api/stream/<id>/audio , so Saaras' live transcript fills the You line as you speak. Silence → after 0.25 s with nothing above the gate (and at least 350 ms of speech in the utterance, so a cough is not a turn) the stream is stopped, the final transcript becomes your turn, and the next stream opens immediately so the ear is never shut while she thinks or speaks. Barge-in → talking while she is speaking is detected at a higher gate (0.05 RMS, versus 0.018 when she is quiet) and cuts her playback instead of waiting for her to finish; the ear stays open and the UI stays on hearing until he stops. Half a second is a short leash , so the continuation rule below earns its keep: a learner who pauses to think mid-sentence gets cut off, keeps talking, and her held answer is folded into the whole sentence instead of a fragment. A pause mid-sentence does not split the turn → if he starts talking again while she is still thinking (before any of her answer has been heard), that answer is held, not spoken over him, and his fragment is carried into the next turn — which goes out as one sentence with replace_previous: true , so the server drops the half-sentence from her history instead of correcting it twice. If the "continuation" turns out to be a cough, the held answer is played after all: no turn is ever lost. The rule lives in static/vad.js as a DOM-free TurnWatcher , so it can be tested without a microphone: node --test # 17 tests: the 0.25 s edge, coughs, room noise, echo, # barge-in vs continuation merge, held replies Thresholds were measured, not guessed: Bulbul speech sits around 0.09 RMS, a quiet room near 0.002, and digital silence at 0.0 — a 40× margin under the gate. echoCancellation , noiseSuppression and autoGainControl are all on for the mic, which is what keeps her own voice out of the turn-taking. Latency Measured against the live API from this machine ( bulbul:v3 , en-IN, one speaker): text characters new connection pooled audio bytes @22 k "What time do you reach office?" 30 0.81 s 0.70 s 2.6 s 87 KB corrected sentence + Hinglish line 110 2.46 s 1.86 s 5.4 s 290 KB two-clause correction 240 4.29 s 3.35 s 15.0 s 527 KB Synthesis is roughly linear in characters (≈14–23 s per 1 000 characters), so the cost is the explanation, not the network. Four things follow: Pooled connections. A fresh TLS handshake per call cost 0.15–0.95 s, and a turn makes two calls → requests.Session with an HTTPAdapter. 16 kHz instead of Bulbul's 22.05 kHz default via speech_sample_rate : 376 KB instead of 592 KB for the same sentence, and 0.5 s quicker. The browser does not need the extra bandwidth. Cap the spoken explanation at 20 words in the prompt: the Hinglish correction is the longest thing she says, and every word is synthesis time. ffmpeg is not the problem — re-encoding a 15 s reply takes 0.07 s. It stays because STT needs a deterministic format, not for speed. Together that moved a turn from 3.4–6.6 s to a median 2.6 s (llm 0.35 s, tts 2.2 s) . The remaining win is streaming: Bulbul can emit audio over a websocket, and playing the first sentence while the second is still being synthesised removes most of the wait the learner actually feels. Deploying The app is one long-lived Python process: sessions in memory, one Sarvam websocket per recording, audio kept in a dict. That is a server , and it rules out pure serverless hosts. Render — free, no Docker. Push the repo, then New → Blueprint and pick this repository: render.yaml builds pip install -r requirements.txt and starts python server.py . Add SARVAM_API_KEY in the dashboard when it asks. The free plan sleeps after ~15 idle minutes, so the first visitor waits ~30 s for a cold start. Any container host (Fly, Railway, Cloud Run, a VPS): docker build -t priyanka . && docker run -p 7860:7860 -e SARVAM_API_KEY=… priyanka . The Dockerfile installs ffmpeg, which the audio normalisation needs. Netlify cannot run this app. The only Netlify primitive that fits is Netlify Server — long-lived, holds websockets, keeps state — and it refuses a Free plan with 422 Netlify Server is only available on credit-based plans . Netlify Functions are JS/TS only, cannot hold the Sarvam websocket across a request, and have no ffmpeg, so a Netlify build would need a JS rewrite and would lose the live transcript. Sessions are per browser (a priyanka_sid cookie), so a shared URL gives each visitor their own tutor. There is no auth: anyone with the link spends the Sarvam key's free tier, so keep the URL to people you know. Why these models Saaras v3 (STT) — built for Indian languages and code-switching. A Hinglish sentence comes back as it was spoken instead of being mangled by an English-only transcriber. The live transcript uses saaras:v3-realtime , the same model over a websocket, so the words on screen are the words the turn runs on. Free API tier. sarvam-105b-conversations (LLM) — the -conversations variant returns the answer in content ; the base sarvam-105b is a reasoning model that hides it in reasoning_content and breaks standard chat clients. Handles the English-conversation and Hinglish-correction mix in one call, and holds the role-play persona turn after turn. Free API tier. Bulbul v3 (TTS) — Indian-English and Hindi voices that pronounce the names and code-switched words correctly. Free API tier. No UI framework — the browser captures with Web Audio, plays the reply through an <audio> element, and talks to a handful of JSON endpoints ( /api/meta , /api/session , /api/turn , /api/summary , /api/preview , /api/stream/* ). server.py is http.server from the standard library, so the app's only dependencies are requests , pyyaml and websockets . Gradio was dropped because it pinned a large dependency tree for a UI that is one page of HTML. Design decisions English is the conversation, Hinglish is the correction. The tutor plays a character and speaks only English; the moment something is wrong — or the learner is stuck — it switches to Hinglish (Hindi in Roman script, mixed with English words) for that one line, then goes back to English: EN: You should say "He goes to school daily." HI: 'He go' ki jagah 'He goes' bolna chahiye, kyunki he ke saath 's' lagta hai. NEXT: EN: What time do you reach office? LEVEL: 1 The correction is its own message. A question wedged into the middle of a correction is what the learner remembers instead of the fix, so NEXT: splits the reply in two: message one is the corrected sentence plus the Hinglish reason and nothing else, message two is the next question. The UI shows them as two bubbles and plays them back to back, and both are synthesised in parallel so the turn still costs the slower of the two rather than the sum. Replies with nothing to correct carry no NEXT: and stay a single message. Lines are spoken in the order written. Both are Latin script, so both go to the en-IN Bulbul voice, which reads code-mixed Indian English naturally; a line that arrives in Devanagari is routed to hi-IN instead. Routing is by script, not by the EN: / HI: tag, because the model sometimes drops the tag — and neighbouring lines in the same language are merged into one TTS request. Segments are synthesised in parallel. Each language segment is its own TTS request; they run concurrently and are stitched back in the written order, so an English+Hinglish reply costs about its slowest segment instead of the sum, and one slow call is retried rather than stalling the turn. Level starts with a confidence question, not a dropdown. The setup has no level picker: the first message asks him to rate his English confidence 1 to 5 (1 = not confident at all, 5 = fully confident). That answer maps onto how hard the tutor comes down on him — 1–2 → almost every mistake in short simple English, 3 → real mistakes plus better wording, 4–5 → naturalness and word choice only — and the tutor re-judges it every turn, reported on a LEVEL: line the parser reads back for the badge. The live transcript is the turn. While the mic is open the page sends 250 ms of 16 kHz PCM to POST /api/stream/<id>/audio ; realtime.py holds one websocket to saaras:v3-realtime per recording and returns whatever transcript.partial events have arrived, so the panel updates as the learner speaks. The key stays on the server — the browser never opens a websocket of its own, and no second port is needed. When the learner stops, a short silence tail flushes the VAD and the transcript.final text is what the turn runs on, so the words on screen are exactly the words the tutor corrects. A MediaRecorder runs alongside as a fallback: if the stream yields nothing the recording is uploaded and transcribed the old way. Long recordings are chunked. Saaras' REST endpoint caps files at 30 s, so longer uploaded recordings are split with ffmpeg and the transcripts joined by the stream instead. Summary comes from the transcript. Ending the session replays the whole conversation to the model with a fixed summarisation prompt — no state to drift. With zero learner turns the model is not called at all: there is nothing to correct, and a model asked to summarise a one-sided conversation invents mistakes. That case returns a fixed, honest blank state instead. Transcripts are kept as spoken. Saaras returns Hinglish in Devanagari ( transcribe mode), which is what the learner actually said; nothing is silently translated. Evaluation python eval_run.py runs 9 scripted learner utterances through the real voice pipeline (TTS → STT → tutor → TTS) and a judge model grades each reply against the expectation for that utterance. 7/9 handled correctly. Average response time 4.1 s (STT 0.9 s · LLM 0.5 s · TTS 2.7 s) on an Intel i7-9750H / 8 GB / Linux, with all three models on Sarvam's cloud — the latency is network + model time, not local compute. A reply is one or two messages of an English line plus a Hinglish correction line; the segments run in parallel and are stitched in order, which is why TTS stays near a single call. # Learner said Verdict Time 1 Mujhe English bolne mein thoda confidence nahi hai, beginner level par hoon. ✅ 3.1s 2 He go to school daily. ✅ 4.1s 3 I am agree with you. ✅ 4.7s 4 Yesterday I go to office and I am explain everything to my manager. ✅ 5.5s 5 mujhe samajh nahi aaya, aap phir se bolo ✅ 3.2s 6 She don't know nothing about the job. ✅ 4.9s 7 Main bahut nervous hoon, interview mein kya bolun? ❌ 3.4s 8 I am working in company from two years. ✅ 4.7s 9 Last weekend I travelled to Jaipur with my cousins and we tried the local street food. ❌ 3.0s Full table, per-turn timings and judge notes: eval/results.md (raw: eval/results.json ). Reproduce with python eval_run.py . The cases cover the confidence answer that sets the level (1), subject–verb agreement (2, 6), "am + verb" (3), past tense (4, 8), a learner stuck in Hinglish (5), a nervous learner who needs a sentence to say (7), and a clean sentence where nothing should be corrected (9). Scores move a point between runs — tutor and judge both sample — so recent runs land at 7–8 of 9. The misses are wording slips (a quote left unclosed, a question that drifted off the learner's topic), never a broken turn: no run has lost a reply or a transcript since the audio path was fixed. Speech-to-text: why mode=codemix The transcript has to keep the learner's mistakes — a tutor that is handed "He goes" can never correct "He go". Measured over 6 fresh recordings of one deliberately ungrammatical sentence: mode grammar silently fixed script transcribe (what this shipped with) 2/6 — returned "He goes … I went … I am explaining" Latin codemix (now used) 0/6 Latin verbatim 0/6 Devanagari — ही गो टू स्कूल, unusable here translate always translates to English Both the batch endpoint and the live websocket ( realtime.py ) now read the same sarvam.STT_MODE , so the two paths cannot drift apart again. Live-path checks over HTTP: transcript returned and marked final, grammar preserved, silence answered in 1.6 s instead of 6 s, and the webm fallback keeping the mistakes — 10/10 in e2e testing. Layout server.py HTTP server + JSON API (stdlib, no framework) realtime.py live transcription: PCM in over HTTP, one websocket to Saaras static/ index.html, style.css, app.js — the whole voice UI static/vad.js turn-taking: silence → turn, barge-in — DOM-free, node-tested static/turns.js continuation + barge-in bookkeeping (merge, hold, replace) tests/ `node --test` — the silence rule and its edge cases tutor.py session state, tutor prompt, turn handling, summary sarvam.py the three Sarvam API clients + audio helpers eval_run.py scripted evaluation → eval/results.{json,md} What I would improve next Latency: TTS still dominates (~1.8 s even with parallel segments). Streaming the reply audio so playback starts on the first sentence, instead of waiting for the whole WAV, would cut the perceived gap again — the input side already streams. True adaptation: the level starts from his own confidence answer and the model re-judges it every turn, so the same mistake can be corrected hard early and left alone later; a spaced-repetition record of each mistake would make practice decisions durable instead of conversational. Pronunciation feedback: Saaras gives text, not phonetics — a scoring pass on the learner's actual audio would catch mispronounced words that are spelled correctly. Offline mode: everything runs on Sarvam's cloud today. A local Whisper + small Hindi-tuned TTS fallback would keep the tutor usable without a network. A MediaRecorder runs alongside as a fallback: if the stream yields nothing the recording is uploaded and transcribed the old way. Long recordings are chunked. Saaras' REST endpoint caps files at 30 s, so longer uploaded recordings are split with ffmpeg and the transcripts joined by the stream instead. Summary comes from the transcript. Ending the session replays the whole conversation to the model with a fixed summarisation prompt — no state to drift. With zero learner turns the model is not called at all: there is nothing to correct, and a model asked to summarise a one-sided conversation invents mistakes. That case returns a fixed, honest blank state instead. Transcripts are kept as spoken. Saaras returns Hinglish in Devanagari ( transcribe mode), which is what the learner actually said; nothing is silently translated. Evaluation python eval_run.py runs 9 scripted learner utterances through the real voice pipeline (TTS → STT → tutor → TTS) and a judge model grades each reply against the expectation for that utterance. 7/9 handled correctly. Average response time 4.1 s (STT 0.9 s · LLM 0.5 s · TTS 2.7 s) on an Intel i7-9750H / 8 GB / Linux, with all three models on Sarvam's cloud — the latency is network + model time, not local compute. A reply is one or two messages of an English line plus a Hinglish correction line; the segments run in parallel and are stitched in order, which is why TTS stays near a single call. # Learner said Verdict Time 1 Mujhe English bolne mein thoda confidence nahi hai, beginner level par hoon. ✅ 3.1s 2 He go to school daily. ✅ 4.1s 3 I am agree with you. ✅ 4.7s 4 Yesterday I go to office and I am explain everything to my manager. ✅ 5.5s 5 mujhe samajh nahi aaya, aap phir se bolo ✅ 3.2s 6 She don't know nothing about the job. ✅ 4.9s 7 Main bahut nervous hoon, interview mein kya bolun? ❌ 3.4s 8 I am working in company from two years. ✅ 4.7s 9 Last weekend I travelled to Jaipur with my cousins and we tried the local street food. ❌ 3.0s Full table, per-turn timings and judge notes: eval/results.md (raw: eval/results.json ). Reproduce with python eval_run.py . The cases cover the confidence answer that sets the level (1), subject–verb agreement (2, 6), "am + verb" (3), past tense (4, 8), a learner stuck in Hinglish (5), a nervous learner who needs a sentence to say (7), and a clean sentence where nothing should be corrected (9). Scores move a point between runs — tutor and judge both sample — so recent runs land at 7–8 of 9. The misses are wording slips (a quote left unclosed, a question that drifted off the learner's topic), never a broken turn: no run has lost a reply or a transcript since the audio path was fixed. Speech-to-text: why mode=codemix The transcript has to keep the learner's mistakes — a tutor that is handed "He goes" can never correct "He go". Measured over 6 fresh recordings of one deliberately ungrammatical sentence: mode grammar silently fixed script transcribe (what this shipped with) 2/6 — returned "He goes … I went … I am explaining" Latin codemix (now used) 0/6 Latin verbatim 0/6 Devanagari — ही गो टू स्कूल, unusable here translate always translates to English Both the batch endpoint and the live websocket ( realtime.py ) now read the same sarvam.STT_MODE , so the two paths cannot drift apart again. Live-path checks over HTTP: transcript returned and marked final, grammar preserved, silence answered in 1.6 s instead of 6 s, and the webm fallback keeping the mistakes — 10/10 in e2e testing. Layout server.py HTTP server + JSON API (stdlib, no framework) realtime.py live transcription: PCM in over HTTP, one websocket to Saaras static/ index.html, style.css, app.js — the whole voice UI static/vad.js turn-taking: silence → turn, barge-in — DOM-free, node-tested static/turns.js continuation + barge-in bookkeeping (merge, hold, replace) tests/ `node --test` — the silence rule and its edge cases tutor.py session state, tutor prompt, turn handling, summary sarvam.py the three Sarvam API clients + audio helpers eval_run.py scripted evaluation → eval/results.{json,md} What I would improve next Latency: TTS still dominates (~1.8 s even with parallel segments). Streaming the reply audio so playback starts on the first sentence, instead of waiting for the whole WAV, would cut the perceived gap again — the input side already streams. True adaptation: the level starts from his own confidence answer and the model re-judges it every turn, so the same mistake can be corrected hard early and left alone later; a spaced-repetition record of each mistake would make practice decisions durable instead of conversational. Pronunciation feedback: Saaras gives text, not phonetics — a scoring pass on the learner's actual audio would catch mispronounced words that are spelled correctly. Offline mode: everything runs on Sarvam's cloud today. A local Whisper + small Hindi-tuned TTS fallback would keep the tutor usable without a network. You can’t perform that action at this time.

Its main mode is Hindi, with Devanagari captions and Sarvam AI narration. English also works. One command takes a story from topic to a finished final_short.mp4 , with a ready-to-paste upload kit (title, description, tags, playlist and captions). How it works topic ──► script ──► fact-check ──► Hindi polish ──► character anchors ──► scenes ──► voice ──► captions ──► render (seed or (Claude) (judge from a (editor model) (Imagen, 1 per (Gemini, (Sarvam (Whisper word (FFmpeg: Ken Burns AI-picked, different model main character) conditioned / TTS) timestamps) motion, music, SFX, deduped by family) on anchors, burned-in captions) embeddings) vision QA) Stage Models (in fallback order) Topic and script claude-sonnet-5-5 → claude-sonnet-4-6 Fact-check judge (different model family) gemini-3.1-pro → gpt-5.4 Hindi editor and fluency judge gemini-3.1-pro / gpt-5.4 (never grades its own edit) Duplicate check text-embedding-3-small (cosine similarity ≥ 0.82 counts as a duplicate) Character anchors (up to 4 per video) imagen-4-ultra → imagen-4 12–14 scenes, conditioned on the anchors gemini-3.1-flash-image → gemini-2.5-flash-image → imagen-4 (text only) Visual QA (text, watermarks, character drift, anatomy) gemini-3.5-flash → gpt-5.4-mini Voice Sarvam Bulbul (Hindi) / tts-1-hd (English) Word timestamps whisper-1, with a pause-anchored fallback Music pick gemini-3.5-flash All text, image and audio calls except Sarvam go through the Fuel iX OpenAI-compatible API. Model chains, thresholds, visual style and seed topics are all set in config.py . Reliability Checkpointed: every output file is a checkpoint. If you rerun after a crash or Ctrl-C, the pipeline skips everything that is already valid on disk. Fallbacks and retries: each stage tries a chain of models. Transient errors (429, 5xx and timeouts) back off and retry. Cost guard: image calls are capped per run ( MAX_IMAGE_CALLS_PER_RUN ), and a circuit breaker stops a batch after too many failures. Run lock and backups: only one run can happen at a time, and the SQLite database is backed up automatically. Requirements Python 3.10+ FFmpeg built with libass (check with ffmpeg -filters | grep subtitles ) A Fuel iX API key, plus a Sarvam AI key for Hindi A Devanagari font (Kohinoor Devanagari ships with macOS; on Linux or Windows use Noto Sans Devanagari) Setup pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # then fill in FUELIX_API_KEY and SARVAM_API_KEY python smoke_test.py # cheap check of text, embeddings, TTS and timestamps python smoke_test.py --images # also tests the anchor, a ref-conditioned scene and vision QA (~3 image calls) If any line says FAIL, that tells you which model name or endpoint to change in config.py . Usage python main.py # produce VIDEOS_TO_GENERATE new videos (finishes interrupted ones first) Topics run in this order: unfinished stories first, then SEED_TOPICS from config.py , then topics the AI picks itself. Other tools Command Purpose python regenerate.py --list Show every story and its status python regenerate.py 1 Re-render story #1 only (no API cost) python regenerate.py 1 --from voice Redo from the given stage onward ( narration , voice , scenes , anchors or script ) python regenerate.py 1 --scene 4 7 Redo only scenes 4 and 7, then re-render python upload_kit.py [N | --all] Build UPLOAD_KIT.txt plus captions in upload_queue/ python bakeoff.py [--edited | --editors] Blind A/B/C/D comparison of writer or editor models python sarvam_voice_test.py [voice ids] Audition Sarvam Hindi voices into voice_samples/ python music.py Check the music library Output Each story gets its own folder, output/NNN_Name/ : script_verified.json fact_check_log.json anchor_c*.png scene_01..14.png voiceover.mp3 subtitles.srt timings.json music_choice.json final_short.mp4 upload_metadata.json UPLOAD_KIT.txt Story status is tracked in data/stories.db , moving through queued → scripted → media_done → rendered . A story that fails MAX_VIDEO_ATTEMPTS times is parked as failed , and the reason is saved in last_error . To retry it: UPDATE stories SET attempts = 0 , status = ' queued ' WHERE id = N; Customising Language: set LANGUAGE = "hi" or "en" in config.py . Voice: put your preferred voice first in SARVAM_VOICES . Visual style: edit TEMPLE_FRESCO_GLOW_STYLE . Hindi name spellings: edit names_hi.json . The writer is told to use these spellings, and any mismatches are corrected afterwards. Viewer feedback on Hindi style: add notes to hindi_feedback.txt . They are fed to the writer and the editor. Music: put instrumental tracks in assets/music/ and list them in assets/music/library.json . Tracks are loudness-normalised, faded and lowered (ducked) under the voice. Sound effects (optional): add assets/sfx/whoosh.mp3 for scene changes and assets/sfx/impact.mp3 for the hook. Fonts: drop a .ttf into assets/fonts/ and set SUBTITLE_FONTS . Settings added in newer versions are filled in from config_defaults.py , so an older config.py keeps working. Project layout File Role main.py Orchestrator: preflight checks, then the resume, seed and AI-topic loop script_engine.py Topic discovery, script writing, validation and the fact-check loop hindi_style.py , names.py Hindi editor, style lint and name normalisation media_generator.py Anchors, scenes, visual QA, voiceover and captions captions.py Word alignment and SRT/ASS caption building (handles Devanagari text shaping) voice.py Sarvam TTS (splits long text into chunks, then joins the WAVs) music.py Music library, LLM track pick and loudness normalisation video_renderer.py FFmpeg rendering: motion, audio mix, hook text, call to action, burned-in captions fuelix_client.py API client: chat, embeddings, images, vision, TTS and transcription db_manager.py SQLite story queue, similarity dedup and backups utils.py Retries, fallbacks, atomic writes and the run lock Security API keys are read only from .env or environment variables. .env is in .gitignore , so it is never committed. Generated media ( output/ , upload_queue/ ), the database ( data/ ), and logs are also excluded. Sarvam AI speech-to-text and translation turn that into a structured cart (items, quantities, pincode), and text-to-speech reads the confirmation back. A marketer dashboard logs the funnel: spoken → parsed → cart → checkout intent. Bolo Bazaar is fictional. The catalogue, prices and demo transcripts are synthetic portfolio data. No orders are placed and no key is ever committed to the repo. Why it matters to a marketer Skill Where it shows up Vernacular / Bharat GTM Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Hinglish aliases on every SKU Voice as a conversion surface Mic → Sarvam saaras:v4 → cart → Bulbul TTS reply Funnel instrumentation In-browser events + CSV export for stakeholder readouts Safe demos Labelled samples work with no API key Modes Demo (default): click a labelled sample. Parsing and the dashboard run fully offline. Sample copy is marked as not a live transcript. Live: paste your own Sarvam API key (stored only in localStorage on your machine). The page calls: POST https://api.sarvam.ai/speech-to-text · model saaras:v4 POST https://api.sarvam.ai/translate POST https://api.sarvam.ai/text-to-speech · model bulbul:v4-flash Auth header: api-subscription-key (see Sarvam quickstart ) Wispr Flow note Wispr Flow is a voice dictation product. Its developer API is not publicly available (partnership / approval only — Wispr’s own note ). This prototype therefore uses the browser microphone + Sarvam, and does not pretend to call Wispr. Try it Open the live demo . Click a demo sample (Hindi / Hinglish / Bengali / Tamil / English). Confirm the cart to record a checkout-intent event; export the CSV from the marketer dashboard. Optional: paste a Sarvam key to try live mic STT and TTS. Run locally python3 -m http.server 8000 # then open http://localhost:8000 # ES modules need a local server — don't open index.html as a file:// URL Tests Cart parsing, demo samples, confirmation copy and funnel CSV helpers: npm install && npm test Project structure index.html UI css/styles.css styles js/catalogue.js synthetic SKUs + aliases js/parser.js order → cart (pure) js/sarvam.js STT / translate / TTS client js/funnel.js localStorage event log js/demo.js labelled sample transcripts js/app.js page wiring docs/product-brief.md tests/parser.test.js License MIT — see LICENSE .
